The COVID-19 context: challenger banks fare well throughout this crisis

The current pandemic being experienced worldwide has been a wake-up call for many sectors in terms of the importance of digitisation. The sanitary crisis has clearly shown us the importance of providing flexible, convenient and quick online services to consumers.

Financial institutions have implemented numerous changes in response to this crisis, such as higher contactless payment limits or delayed loan repayments. More than ever before, consumers needed to be able to manage all aspects of their financial life online. According to an MX survey conducted in the United States: 59% of people are spending less money than before due to COVID-19, 55% use their mobile app as a primary tool to check their account balance and only 2% are going to their bank’s branch. We asked Jörg how the crisis has impacted Neon thus far:

“At Neon we see three different areas impacted by COVID 19: increasing demand from new clients opening a Neon account, distinct shifts in the payment behaviour of existing clients (fewer cash transactions, more contactless payments, increase in average transaction amount, different shopping behaviour, etc.) and of course different ways of working together within our team and with our several partners.”

The coronavirus crisis and the conversations it has sparked will indubitably provide food for thought to financial institutions worldwide. Challenger banks, which were already well prepared for this type of situation without even knowing it, could likely continue to experience fast growth linked to the currently shifting consumer behaviour.

Small loans on benefits may be available for self-employed individuals, depending on the specific lender and their criteria. What happens if I miss a repayment on a small loan on benefits?

If you miss a repayment on a small loan while on benefits, the consequences may vary depending on the terms and conditions of the loan agreement and the lending institution's policies. However, here are some general things that may happen in such a situation:

  1. Late Payment Fees: Typically, lenders apply late payment fees or additional charges for missed or delayed loan repayments. These fees can add to the overall cost of the loan.
  2. Increased Interest Rates: Some lenders may increase the interest rate on your loan if you miss a repayment. This can significantly impact the total amount you owe over the loan term.
  3. Negative Impact on Credit Score: Being late or missing loan repayments can negatively impact your credit score. This may make it difficult for you to secure credit in the future, as lenders consider your credit history when evaluating loan applications.
  4. Collection Efforts: Lenders may take steps to recover the amount owed. This can include sending collection letters or contacting you via phone or email to remind you of the missed payment and request immediate repayment.
  5. Legal Actions: In extreme cases, lenders may take legal actions against borrowers who consistently fail to make loan repayments. This can result in court proceedings, wage garnishment, or asset seizure, depending on the jurisdiction and the specific circumstances.

If you anticipate difficulties in making loan repayments, it is always advisable to proactively contact your lender and discuss the situation. They may provide some solutions such as adjusting the repayment schedule or offering alternative repayment arrangements.

After you e-file your return, you should next figure out how quickly you can pay off your entire tax bill. How long will it take you to pay off what you owe to the IRS?

Figuring out the amount of time it will take to satisfy your debt serves two purposes. First, it helps you budget accordingly for paying off your tax bill over a set amount of time. Second, it allows you to get a head start on requesting an installment agreement from the IRS if you need one.

If the tax bill is relatively small, you may be able to pay off what you owe in one or two payments. However, when it is hundreds or thousands of dollars, you may need to request an installment agreement from the IRS. You should use IRS Form 9465 to request an installment agreement in writing.

If you owe a large debt to the IRS, you should contact it immediately to make arrangements to pay off the obligation. Once you are set up on a payment arrangement, you can use a credit or debit card to have the monthly payments deducted automatically for you. Alternatively, you can send in a check or money order to the IRS each month to pay on your debt.

If you use a credit or debit card, however, your payments are received and credited the same day you make the payment. If you mail in a check or money order, it may be a week or longer before your payment is credited to your debt. Immediate acceptance of your payment can be crucial to avoiding anymore penalties or interest on what you already owe.

RESMARK Systems was started to meet the needs of two companies: Western River Expeditions, and Moab Adventure Center. 13) “With the Coronavirus On the Loose, How Do We Go Paperless?”

Speaking of pandemics, you may be concerned about that, either because you're personally worried about the spread of the virus, or because you want to accommodate guests who are. That’s fair. All other factors aside, no one really likes getting sick, and cutting down on the risk of spreading a highly contagious disease is always a good idea.

Part of that reduction of risk can be done by going "contactless" or "paperless" in your transactions. But how might a business achieve such a thing?

Our Answer

Ok, so maybe we're not the only provider who might say this, but our whole system is designed to be free of contact. Guests can make reservations online, check in via mobile (like, you know, the one they brought with them), sign waivers online or via mobile, and even provide reviews and testimonials, all without paper or physical contact.

While this obviously won't remove all the risk related to Coronavirus (you'll still need waivers to handle some of that), it will certainly keep you, your staff, and your guests safer, and that’s got to be worth something.

@ rom - take the analogy of using your web browser to connect to an internet bank or e-commerce website, which protects your financial details over the internet using a Secure Sockets layer (SSL) or Transaction Layer Security (TLS) encrypted session.

Your local network administrator or your Internet Service Provider cannot read your banking or credit card transactions because of the encryption, but they absolutely and routinely do know on what date and at which time and which IP address or URL you used to connect to the secure website, information which they may hand over to someone else either for law enforcement reasons, or simply for money.

Similarly with "proximity" or "contactless" or "RFID" smartcards or tags or tickets etc. the reader equipment has to be able to distinguish between two or more smartcards or tags which happen to be within range of the permitted strength radio signal ("collision avoidance"), otherwise, just as with an IP address on a computer network, some or all of the wrong data will end up at the wrong network card, usually preventing either of the non-uniquely addressed devices from working properly.

There are already various commercial marketing experiments in tracking unsuspecting individual members of the public, which are illegal in the UK because they do not obtain the explicit, individual's informed consent first, according to the Principles of Data Protection enshrined in the Data Protection Act e.g.

  • tracking BlueTooth mobile phones, of repeat "high value" customers visitors in a department store,

  • using the same technology to activate an "intelligent" advertising billboard display,
  • using GSM mobile phones carried by car drivers to estimate traffic flows and traffic jams for the benefit of paying customers, but not of the people whose traffic movements have been snooped on
  • snooping on the radio station to which car drivers have their radios tuned to e.g. pop, classical or news etc. again for
